ACMC LEADERSHIP
Ivan Vashchenko
Founder & President
Applied Computational Modeling Club (ACMC)
was established in Spring 2025 with one mission: to
build a professional, execution-first environment
where students develop high-demand skills, and
leave college with a portfolio and network that actu-
ally mean something.
ACMC didn’t become what it is by accident. We’ve
grown through iteration: trying ideas, learning fast,
and keeping what genuinely resonates. Over the past
three semesters, we’ve hosted discussions, technical
workshops, hackathons and entrepreneurship com-
petitions, lectures and conferences, but the core
of ACMC has always been the same: teams building
projects under real deadlines, and then showing the
work publicly.
My name is Ivan Vashchenko, and I’m the Founder
and President of ACMC. I care deeply about creating
opportunities that help students stand out through
output, clear communication, and high standards.
ACMC is still evolving, and that’s intentional. Our mis-
sion stays constant; our methods keep improving.
Welcome to The ACMC Chronicle (Spring 2026 ·
Annual Edition No. 1) Inside, you’ll meet the people
who shaped ACMC, see the projects we shipped,
and get a clear picture of what we’re building: an
interdisciplinary organization designed to execute,
learn fast, and keep raising the bar.

Prem Pun Magar
Technical Lead
As Technical Lead, Club Coordinator, and head of
the Robotics Department, Prem Pun Magar has
been a foundational presence in ACMC from the
very beginning, involved in shaping the club’s mis-
sion before it even took off. He has helped define
what ACMC actually does and what kind of people
it is built for. “The reason we started ACMC was sim-
ple, to build things,” he says. “A year and a half later, I
can confidently say we have built that identity”
As co-ordinator, Prem has helped give structure to
the club through workshops, and projects. He has
also been a consistent presence at every hackathon
that ACMC has entered, not just as a builder but as
someone who has helped the team stay focused
under pressure. His belief that ACMC should be a
place for everyone and not just computer science
students has helped influence how the club grows.
This perspective continues to shape what ACMC
has become.
ACMC LEADERSHIP
Jonathan Langton
Faculty Advisor
Dr. Jonathan Langton has been ACMC’s
faculty advisor since the start of the club. The idea
of ACMC came partly from the dynamics course he
taught where some students came across encoun-
tered computational problems that sparked early
conversations with current president and founder
Ivan Vashchenko about what the club could poten-
tially look like. Since then, Dr. Langton has served as
a constant presence behind the last three semes-
ters, offering guidance when needed.
Dr. Jonathan Langton holds a PhD degree in phys-
ics from the University of Santa Cruz in California
and has spent 16 years teaching physics, mathemat-
ics and engineering courses at Principia College.

The Voice of ACMC
Such a rapid success and quick recognition of ACMC would never happen without
a well-structured marketing team that started leading with ownership and creativity
from day one of the existence of ACMC. Isaac and Jackie joined as ACMC’s brand
manager and public relations marketer.
Isaac Salas Jackie Reyes
ACMC Brand Manager ACMC Public Relations Marketer
People did not really understand what ACMC was. The name
sounded technical. The work looked technical. And for a
lot of students, that was enough to stay away. That is where
Isaac Salas and Jackie Reyes came in. They stepped into
the role early, when the club was still figuring itself out. The
challenge was not just to promote ACMC. It was to explain it.
How events were presented. How people talked about the
work. And how to make it feel like something you could be
part of, even if you had never written a line of code before.
What is computational modeling? Why does it matter? And
why should anyone outside of computer science care?
Those questions had to be answered before anything else.
From the start, the goal was clear. Make ACMC feel innova-
tive, but also approachable.
At the beginning, that was not easy. “The biggest challenge
was that no one really knew what ACMC was yet,” Salas ex-
plains. “We had to communicate both the idea of the club
and why it mattered.” Over time, that started to work. More
people showed up. Meetings grew. Showcases brought in
students and faculty who wanted to see what was being built.
ACMC became something people on campus recognized.
“I didn’t want it to look like just another technical club that
only programmers could join,” Salas says. “It had to feel like a
place where anyone curious could come in and build.” That
meant thinking about how the club showed up.
That did not happen in one moment. It came from consistent
effort. Communicating clearly. Showing the work. Making sure
people understood what was actually going on. In the end, the
marketing team did more than promote ACMC. They gave it
a voice.

The Builders OF ACMC
BUILDERS
Ideas are easy. Execution is the hard part. At ACMC, the software department is where
that gap gets closed, where concepts move off whiteboards and into working proto-
types, where teams stay up late debugging, and where students discover what they are
actually capable of building. The majority of ACMC’s members pass through this space
at some point, contributing to projects, competing at hackathons, and generating the
kind of startup-like thinking that defines the club’s identity.
Kesiena Berezi
Software Developer
Senior Kesiena Berezi has been part of ACMC’s growth. From the early days
of the club to its most recent hackathon, he has consistently been one of the
people helping turn ideas into a working project. Berezi’s role extended be-
yond building things, or making things work. As the team grew, many projects
began to bring together students with different levels of programming ex-
perience, which meant someone had to help keep the team moving forward.
“When you’re working with people who are newer to development, you have
to explain not just what you’re doing, but why you’re doing it,” Berezi says.
“Otherwise it can feel overwhelming.”
Balancing mentorship with the time pressure of hackathons is never simple.
With only a limited number of hours to move from idea to prototype, teams
often have to make quick decisions while still keeping everyone involved.
For Berezi, the key has always been structure and accountability. “Proper
planning, breaking down the roles of everybody, and holding each other ac-
countable,” he says. “That’s the key to success. Everyone has to carry their
own weight. That mindset has helped create an environment at ACMC where
new members can step into serious work quickly and learn how real collabo-
ration works.
Sana Udoekong
Software Developer
Sophomore Sana Udoekong joined in the fall of 2025, stepping into a de-
partment with high expectations. She came with a willingness to engage
with the process seriously from the start. Instead of waiting for experience to
come first, she embraced the idea that experience is something you gain by
doing the work. For Udoekong, the club quickly became a lesson in how col-
laborative building actually works, how teams think through problems, adapt
when plans change, and push projects forward.

ACMC in the World: Hackathons
Hackathons became an important part of ACMC’s growth
from the very beginning. They gave members a chance to
take what they were learning in class and apply it in fast, de-
manding, real-world settings. In a short amount of time, teams
had to move from an idea to a working product, make design
decisions under pressure, divide responsibilities clearly, and
present their work in a convincing way. For many ACMC
members, this experience added a practical dimension to
classroom knowledge and pushed them to learn beyond
the pace of a regular course.
Hackathons
Over the last three semesters, ACMC teams represented Prin-
cipia at several hackathons and worked on projects across a
wide range of themes and technical challenges. These experi-
ences gave students the opportunity to build under pressure,
collaborate closely, and see what it takes to develop a project
from concept to presentation within a very limited amount
of time. They also helped establish hackathons as one of the
most valuable spaces for ACMC members to grow
technically, creatively, and professionally.
Hackathons also created opportunities outside of the tech-
nical work itself. ACMC members connected with students
from other universities, mentors, organizers, and professionals
from industry. They were exposed to stronger competition,
different approaches to problem-solving, and the level of
execution expected in larger innovation spaces.
This became especially clear at the LIVE AI Ivy Plus
Hackathon, where ACMC’s project Argus received six
recognitions: Best Demo — Global Winner; Global Fintech
— 2nd Place; Global Overall — Honorable Mention; Global
AI Track — Honorable Mention; Best Product — Honorable
Mention; Best Design — Honorable Mention. Argus is also be-
ing evaluated by Converge Accelerator for up to $25,000 in
investment. For ACMC, hackathons became a place to build,
test ideas, represent Principia, and grow as a team.

PROJECTS
Projects are the way ACMC members express themselves, explore their interests, and address concerns and problems they
care about. Software applications can now be used as tools to solve a very broad range of problems, and ACMC members did
not limit their imagination when building things that bridge gaps between people, industries, and ideas.
Throughout the last three semesters, ACMC members built a social media platform designed to foster better conversations
and unity by minimizing polarization; an app for tracking CO2 emissions produced by users’ regular trips to work, grocery
stores, and school; a payment guard that checks transactions for fraud and evaluates the intent behind each payment; an art
visualization of gravitational and magnetic force relationships between particles; and a system that detects AI-generated and
deepfake images and videos while also checking the factual validity of social media posts. These are only a few examples.
Each member had an opportunity to build things they genuinely care about, while working in a team. Some of these projects
were more sophisticated from a coding standpoint, while others carried deeper meaning for the team building them. Some
served as training and learning experiences, while others became impressive demonstrations that required teams to think
deeply about design, coordination, and implementation.
Voice Cloner was one of ACMC’s earliest projects, built by Ivan and Prem during the club’s first hackathon at eHacks @SIUE in spring
2025. It used machine learning to analyze and replicate speech patterns and became an important early step in ACMC’s growth.
MagnetiFlow is a physics-based generative art project where colorful particles move across a canvas under gravitational and magnetic
forces. As they interact, they create shifting patterns that make science visual, dynamic, and artistic.
EcoTrail AI was built to make everyday envi-
ronmental impact easier to understand. Users
enter their regular trips, and the system maps
routes, estimates CO2 emissions, and provides
feedback on how daily travel habits can become
more sustainable.
TrustCard is an AI-powered content verification
system designed to respond to misinformation.
It checks social media posts for deepfake media,
fact-checks claims, and generates a clear trust
report to help users judge whether content is
reliable.
Scene was designed to solve a simple but
familiar problem. Instead of scrolling through
hundreds of shared event photos, users upload a
photo of themselves and the platform finds the
pictures where they appear.

Sustainability Science Around the World
You’ll never walk alone - ACMC Partners
The very first conversation between the Center for Business and Computer Science (CBCS) and ACMC started in the fall of
2025. Dr. Lucia De Paz, the director of CBCS, did not need that much convincing before deciding to partner with ACMC.
“The authenticity was there, the desire was there, the passion was there” she said. “That’s what we should be focused on.”
De Paz's role at CBCS was built around one main idea which was to be an enabler. Her role was not to run the show, or to
take over but, it was to make sure that when students came over with ideas, the institution was there to help them achieve it.
De Paz is thinking big about the club and she wants the club to do the same. “Bigger, bolder, better” she says. “We’re here to
have that conversation and see how we can make these big dreams come true.” One of those plans is hosting a hackathon
here at Principia campus. The proposal is already in motion. Hosting an event of that scale requires more than one good
idea. It takes planning, resources and the right support system.
That support came from someone who has been at ACMC before the very first meeting. Beyond his role as faculty advisor,
Dr.Jonathan Langton is a co-founder of Science Around the World, a non-profit organization focused on expanding ac-
cess to science education around the world. The organization works to create opportunities for students around the world
who don’t have access to good learning environments.
“When I think about the experience I had going through school, and the experience students have here,” he says, “I think
it’s important to try to spread those more widely”
When the conversation around hosting a campus hackathon began to take shape, he saw it as an opportunity for the
non-profit to play a role in reaching out to potential sponsors. “It’s very much at the outset of the planning stage,” Langton
says. “But I think it’s something we’ll both be learning a lot about as things begin to move forward.”
For ACMC, the club has never waited until everything was perfectly in place before moving forward. It builds, learns and
figures out along the way. With the help of CBCS and Science Around the World, the foundation is already there.
After attending a hackathon at Washington University in St. Louis, where one of the teams built EcoTrail AI, an idea
emerged within ACMC leadership: projects like this could be developed further and used to benefit the Principia com-
munity and different departments, particularly Sustainability in the case of EcoTrail AI. This started a conversation between
ACMC and the Sustainability Department.
Currently, ACMC and the Sustainability Department are in the process of identifying data science-related projects where
ACMC members can provide support while also gaining valuable experience.
